subject.name_or_desc: A well-affected person (a Parliament sympathiser), asking Lilly

context.question: Is the news/report true — has the King taken Cambridge?
context.asked_at: 1643 (exact day not stated in the text)
context.setting: 1643, during the Civil War: reports were circulating that the King's forces had taken Cambridge

attachments.key_positions: All angles moveable; Saturn vitiating the cusp of the 10th and Mars the cusp of the 7th (per Lilly's prose); Moon cadent in a sign 'wherein she nothing delights'; Sun on the cusp of the Ascendant; lady of the Ascendant (significatrix of the querent side / Parliament) in her exaltation; lord of the 7th (the King's side) entering his fall and afflicted
attachments.note: Positions as stated in Lilly's prose judgment.

master_predictions.statement_excerpt: The report is false: 'All that we heard was untruth, and the Town neither was, or should be taken by Him or his Forces'; the news were lies, devolving to division among the enemy and no benefit to them.
master_predictions.source: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II，Book II, Chap. XXXI 'If a Report or common Rumour were True or False' (1647 pp.204–208)
key_assertions: 传闻不实：剑桥未被国王攻取、也不会被其攻取
消息是谎言，只会带来敌方内部分裂、对敌方无益

outcome.description: Not stated as a postscript in the excerpt, but a matter of historical record: Cambridge was never taken by the King during the Civil War (it remained a Parliamentarian stronghold, headquarters of the Eastern Association). Marked as externally verified, not Lilly-stated.
outcome.verified_by: 外部史实核对（原书节录未另载应验后记）

provenance.book: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (1647), Book II
provenance.edition: 1647 first edition (Internet Archive scan OCR); wording cross-checked against the 1852 Zadkiel edition where noted
